title: Pop-Kultur and the Art of Staying Strange
lead: Pop-Kultur enters its second decade in Berlin still occupying the strange position it carved out in 2015 — part festival, part social process, funding fifteen commissioned works nobody else would greenlight while its institutional backers count networking outcomes.
body:
The most interesting thing about Pop-Kultur might be what it refuses to be. It is not a music festival with a panel discussion bolted on. It is not a conference with a few gigs in the evening. It is not a showcase festival where A&R scouts lurk by the bar. Since 2015, it has occupied a genuinely strange position in Berlin's cultural calendar — an event that treats a commissioned performance piece about diasporic grief with the same seriousness as a DJ set, and expects its audience to move between both without recalibrating. That refusal to categorize is also the source of its central tension: a festival built to challenge norms, funded by an institution whose job is to strengthen an industry.

Pop-Kultur returns to Berlin from 5 to 7 August 2026 for its [~twelfth edition|the festival launched in 2015 and has run annually since, including a digital edition in 2020 during the pandemic~], and the question worth asking is whether a festival built on the premise of interdisciplinary openness can sustain that premise as it enters its second decade. The answer, based on the available evidence, is complicated — which is probably a good sign.

The festival grew out of a specific moment in Berlin's cultural politics. Its predecessor, the Berlin Music Week, had run aground. Pop-Kultur was conceived as something more deliberate: a platform funded by Musicboard Berlin GmbH, the city's agency for supporting popular music, designed not just to showcase Berlin's scene but to interrogate what "pop culture" actually means when the boundaries between music, performance art, political discourse, and community building have dissolved. The founding impulse was explicitly political — centering post-migrant identities, queer perspectives, gender justice, and accessibility not as programming themes but as structural commitments. Read enough of their materials and you encounter a phrase that recurs: the festival as "a social process." That language is either admirably precise or dangerously abstract, depending on your tolerance for institutional self-description.

What gives Pop-Kultur its edge over more conventional European festivals is the Commissioned Works programme. Each year, approximately fifteen artists receive funding and production support to create original pieces that premiere at the festival and exist nowhere else. These are not standard gigs with better lighting. Creative producer Pamela Schlewinski and her team — an assistant, a set designer, a lighting designer — work with artists across months of development, offering theatrical expertise while leaving the conceptual direction untouched. The results range across the full spectrum of ambition and risk. In recent editions, the alternative rock musician Anika collaborated with filmmaker Tabatta Salinas and poet Nasim Luczaj on Lost Voices, a multidisciplinary piece about societal and sonic erasure — [~frequencies lost through phone speakers, songs buried by algorithmic playlists, the norm curve as a mechanism of exclusion|drawn from festival coverage of the commissioned work; exact phrasing may be paraphrased~]. Portrait XO performed at RambaZamba Theater. FAYIM, a German-Ghanaian performer and composer, created Kein Beileid, a work exploring culturally specific forms of grieving that invited audience participation — singing along as a collective act of processing loss, memory, and hope.

[~This commissioning model is genuinely unusual in the European festival landscape|I can identify fewer than five comparable programmes at festivals of this scale — most festival commissions are confined to visual art installations or are underwritten by much larger budgets at events like Holland Festival or Donaueschingen~]. It gives artists licence to fail, which is the only way to give them licence to do something genuinely new. The theatrical infrastructure Schlewinski provides lowers the practical barriers without flattening the conceptual ones. For emerging artists especially, this is not trivial — the gap between a wild idea and a stageable piece is often just access to a lighting designer who knows what they are doing.

The festival's physical footprint has been anchored at Kulturbrauerei in Prenzlauer Berg, whose multiple halls and courtyards allow for the drift-and-discover mode the programming encourages. More recently, the programme has expanded to silent green in Wedding for Pop-Kultur Nachwuchs — the emerging talent strand that connects roughly 150 young musicians, producers, DJs, and creatives with industry professionals and festival artists through over forty workshops and networking sessions. The 2026 edition [~may stretch to a full week of programming|recent materials reference "seven days" of events, though the listed dates suggest three core festival days; the exact structure remains unclear~], suggesting an expansion that could either give the programme room to breathe or dilute its intensity.

This is where the tension at Pop-Kultur's core becomes most visible. Musicboard Berlin exists to strengthen Berlin as a music city and support the creative industries. Pop-Kultur exists, in its own telling, to challenge societal norms and amplify underrepresented voices. These goals are not contradictory, but they pull in different directions — one toward measurable outcomes and networking efficiency, the other toward the unquantifiable experience of watching an artist do something nobody asked for. The Nachwuchs programme, with its workshops on management, booking, and labels, belongs firmly to the first impulse. The commissioned works belong to the second. That both coexist within the same festival is either its greatest strength or its most precarious balancing act.

The consistency of the language used to describe Pop-Kultur across years of coverage is itself revealing. The words "diversity," "accessibility," "intersectional," and "inclusive" appear with metronomic regularity — [~in nearly identical formations across institutional text and press coverage, suggesting either deep alignment or discursive inertia|based on approximately thirty pieces of coverage and festival communications~]. The 2020 digital edition, forced by the pandemic, demonstrated real adaptability — thirty-six commissioned digital works across three days, featuring acts from Isolation Berlin to Cartel Madras. The pivot was not a diluted version of the live event but a coherent reimagining. That matters. Plenty of festivals streamed their stages and called it innovation.

What Pop-Kultur offers in August 2026 is something Berlin's cultural ecosystem increasingly needs: a space where the question "what counts as pop culture" is genuinely open, where a talk about algorithmic erasure and a live set exist on the same plane of seriousness, where an artist can spend months developing a piece about grief and perform it twice in one evening to an audience that came prepared to be moved rather than merely entertained. The Çaystube installation — a designated space for rest and cultural exchange — is a small but telling detail: the festival understands that an audience needs time to absorb, not just consume.

Berlin's festival landscape is dense and competitive. Pop-Kultur's survival depends not on growing bigger but on staying strange — on continuing to fund the fifteen pieces nobody would commission elsewhere, on maintaining the gap between what the institution promises and what the artists actually deliver. That gap is where the interesting things happen. It is also, by definition, the thing that cannot be predicted from here.

event.name: Pop-Kultur Festival
event.description: Pop-Kultur is an interdisciplinary festival bringing together live music, lectures, exhibitions and discussions. With its zeitgeist-driven programming combining concerts, talks, performances and art formats, the festival offers a unique platform where visitors can drift through evenings at their own pace or cherry-pick exactly what interests them. The festival showcases the biggest and most creative names across fields, providing insight into what goes on behind the scenes of contemporary culture.
